title: Materials: Metals and Non-Metals
description: Grade 8 Science: physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals, reactions with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions (displacement), and their uses.

topics.title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-Metals
topics.concept:
All the elements around us can be broadly divided into metals and non-metals, based on their properties. We can tell them apart first by their physical properties.

Metals (such as iron, copper, aluminium, gold) usually:

  • are lustrous (shiny) when freshly cut;
  • are hard and strong (except a few like sodium);
  • are malleable — can be beaten into thin sheets;
  • are ductile — can be drawn into thin wires;
  • are good conductors of heat and electricity;
  • are sonorous — make a ringing sound when struck;
  • generally have high melting points and are solids at room temperature (mercury is a liquid metal).

Non-metals (such as carbon, sulphur, oxygen, iodine) usually have the opposite properties: they are dull (not shiny), soft or brittle (break easily), poor conductors of heat and electricity, not sonorous, and may be solids, liquids or gases at room temperature.

There are a few exceptions that you must remember: iodine is a non-metal but is lustrous; graphite (a form of carbon) is a non-metal but conducts electricity; and diamond (also carbon) is the hardest natural substance though it is a non-metal.

examples.problem: Example 1: What do the terms malleable and ductile mean?
examples.solution:
Both describe how metals can be shaped.

  • Malleable — can be beaten into thin sheets.
  • Ductile — can be drawn into thin wires.
examples.answer: Malleable means it can be beaten into sheets; ductile means it can be drawn into wires.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give two physical properties that help you identify a non-metal.
examples.solution:
Non-metals are mostly the opposite of metals.

  • They are dull (not shiny) and brittle (break easily).
  • They are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
examples.answer: Non-metals are usually dull and brittle, and they are poor conductors of heat and electricity.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name one non-metal that is an exception to the usual properties, and say why.
examples.solution:
A few non-metals behave like metals in one way.

  • Graphite (carbon) is a non-metal but conducts electricity.
  • (Iodine is a non-metal but is lustrous; diamond is very hard.)
examples.answer: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity (or iodine, a non-metal that is lustrous; diamond, very hard).

recap:
• Metals are lustrous, hard, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Non-metals are dull, brittle/soft, non-sonorous and poor conductors.
  • Malleable = beaten into sheets; ductile = drawn into wires.
  • Exceptions: iodine (lustrous), graphite (conducts electricity), diamond (very hard) — all non-metals.

quiz.q: The property of a metal that lets it be drawn into thin wires is called:
quiz.explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires.

quiz.q: Which non-metal is an exception because it conducts electricity?
quiz.explanation: Graphite, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts electricity.

topics.title: Chemical Properties of Metals and Non-Metals
topics.concept:
Metals and non-metals also differ in how they react with other substances — their chemical properties.

  • Reaction with oxygen: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are basic in nature. Non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides, which are acidic. For example, magnesium burns in air to form magnesium oxide (basic), while sulphur burns to form sulphur dioxide (acidic).
  • Reaction with water: Some metals react with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Very reactive metals like sodium react violently even with cold water, while many non-metals do not react with water at all.
  • Reaction with acids: Metals react with dilute acids to give a salt and release hydrogen gas (seen as bubbles). Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids.
  • Displacement reactions: A more reactive metal can push out (displace) a less reactive metal from its salt solution. For example, iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution, and the blue solution slowly turns greenish while a brown coating of copper forms on the iron.

The order of metals from most to least reactive is called the reactivity series. It helps us predict which metal will displace another and how vigorously a metal will react.

examples.problem: Example 1: When a metal reacts with a dilute acid, which gas is released? How can you test for it?
examples.solution:
Metals release a specific gas with acids.

  • Hydrogen gas is released (seen as bubbles).
  • It is tested by bringing a burning splint near it — it burns with a 'pop' sound.
examples.answer: Hydrogen gas is released; it gives a 'pop' sound when a burning splint is brought near it.

examples.problem: Example 2: An iron nail is dipped in blue copper sulphate solution. What change is seen, and why?
examples.solution:
Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it.

  • Iron displaces copper from the solution.
  • A brown coating of copper forms on the nail and the blue colour fades to greenish.
examples.answer: A brown copper coating forms on the nail and the blue solution turns greenish, because the more reactive iron displaces copper.

examples.problem: Example 3: Magnesium oxide and sulphur dioxide are both oxides. How do they differ in nature?
examples.solution:
Metal oxides and non-metal oxides differ in acidity.

  • Magnesium oxide is a metal oxide — it is basic.
  • Sulphur dioxide is a non-metal oxide — it is acidic.
examples.answer: Magnesium oxide (a metal oxide) is basic, while sulphur dioxide (a non-metal oxide) is acidic.

recap:
• Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.
  • Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas (pop test); non-metals usually do not.
  • Reactive metals (e.g. sodium) react with water; many non-metals do not.
  • A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution (iron displaces copper); the reactivity series ranks metals by reactivity.

quiz.q: When most metals react with a dilute acid, the gas released is:
quiz.explanation: Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas.

quiz.q: Metal oxides are generally ___ in nature, while non-metal oxides are ___.
quiz.explanation: Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.

topics.title: Uses of Metals and Non-Metals
topics.concept:
Because of their useful properties, metals and non-metals are used everywhere in daily life and industry.

Uses of metals:

  • Iron and steel — for making machines, vehicles, tools, bridges and buildings (they are strong).
  • Copper and aluminium — for electrical wires (they are good conductors); aluminium is also used in foil and cooking pots because it is light.
  • Gold and silver — for jewellery (they are shiny and do not corrode easily).
  • Metals are used to make cooking utensils because they conduct heat well.

Uses of non-metals:

  • Oxygen — needed by all living things for breathing (respiration) and for burning fuels.
  • Nitrogen — used in fertilisers to help plants grow.
  • Carbon — graphite is used in pencil leads, diamond in cutting tools and jewellery.
  • Chlorine — used to purify (disinfect) drinking water; iodine is used as an antiseptic on wounds.

Some metals react with air and moisture and slowly get spoilt — for example iron forms a brown layer of rust. To prevent rusting we apply paint, grease or a coating of another metal (such as zinc, in a process called galvanisation). Knowing the properties of metals and non-metals helps us choose the right material for each job and protect them from damage.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is copper used for electrical wires while iron is used for building bridges?
examples.solution:
Each metal is chosen for a useful property.

  • Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity → wires.
  • Iron is strong and hard → bridges and structures.
examples.answer: Copper is used for wires because it conducts electricity well, while iron is used for bridges because it is strong.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name two non-metals and give one important use of each.
examples.solution:
Pick non-metals with everyday uses.

  • Oxygen — needed for breathing.
  • Chlorine — used to purify drinking water.
examples.answer: Oxygen (for breathing) and chlorine (to purify drinking water); other answers like nitrogen for fertilisers are also correct.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is galvanisation, and why is it done?
examples.solution:
Galvanisation protects iron from rusting.

  • It is coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc.
  • The zinc layer stops air and moisture from reaching the iron, preventing rust.
examples.answer: Galvanisation is coating iron with zinc to protect it from rusting by keeping out air and moisture.

recap:
• Metals: iron/steel (strong — machines, buildings), copper/aluminium (conductors — wires), gold/silver (jewellery).
  • Non-metals: oxygen (breathing), nitrogen (fertilisers), carbon (graphite/diamond), chlorine (water), iodine (antiseptic).
  • Iron forms rust in air and moisture.
  • Rusting is prevented by paint, grease or galvanisation (zinc coating).

quiz.q: Which non-metal is used to disinfect drinking water?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine is used to purify (disinfect) drinking water.

quiz.q: Coating iron with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting is called:
quiz.explanation: Galvanisation is coating iron with zinc to stop it rusting.

questions.q: Which of these is a property of most metals?
questions.explanation: Metals are usually shiny (lustrous) and malleable.

questions.q: The ability of a metal to be beaten into thin sheets is called:
questions.explanation: Malleability is the ability to be beaten into sheets.

questions.q: Metals make a ringing sound when struck. This property is called:
questions.explanation: Making a ringing sound when struck is sonority.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-metal?
questions.explanation: Sulphur is a non-metal; the others are metals.

questions.q: Graphite is an unusual non-metal because it:
questions.explanation: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity, an exception.

questions.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury is the only common metal that is a liquid at room temperature.

questions.q: Metal oxides are generally:
questions.explanation: Metal oxides are basic in nature.

questions.q: Non-metal oxides are generally:
questions.explanation: Non-metal oxides are acidic in nature.

questions.q: When a metal reacts with a dilute acid, it usually releases:
questions.explanation: Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas.

questions.q: An iron nail dipped in copper sulphate solution gets a ___ coating.
questions.explanation: Iron displaces copper, which deposits as a brown coating on the nail.

questions.q: A more reactive metal pushing out a less reactive metal from its salt solution is a:
questions.explanation: This is a displacement reaction, predicted by the reactivity series.

questions.q: Copper and aluminium are widely used for electrical wires because they are:
questions.explanation: They are good conductors of electricity.

questions.q: Which non-metal is needed by all living things for respiration?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is needed for breathing (respiration).

questions.q: The brown layer formed on iron in moist air is called:
questions.explanation: Iron forms rust in the presence of air and moisture.

questions.q: Coating iron with zinc to prevent rusting is called:
questions.explanation: Galvanisation coats iron with zinc to prevent rusting.

questions.q: Sodium is stored under kerosene oil because it:
options: Reacts vigorously with the moisture and oxygen in air
questions.explanation: Sodium is so reactive it catches fire with air/water, so it is kept under kerosene.

questions.q: A piece of zinc is added to copper sulphate solution but copper is NOT added to zinc sulphate solution that reacts. This shows that:
options: Zinc is more reactive than copper
Copper is more reactive than zinc
questions.explanation: Only a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one; zinc displaces copper, so zinc is more reactive.

questions.q: Why does food cooked in an iron pan add some iron to our diet but a copper vessel must be used with care?
options: Metals can slowly react with food; iron is helpful but excess copper salts are harmful
Copper has no effect at all
questions.explanation: Metals can react slightly with food; small iron is beneficial, but copper compounds in excess can be harmful.

questions.q: Sulphur dioxide gas dissolves in rain water to form acid rain. This is because the oxide of a non-metal is:
questions.explanation: Non-metal oxides are acidic, so SO2 makes rain water acidic.

questions.q: Aluminium does not rust away like iron even though it is reactive, because:
options: A thin oxide layer forms and protects the metal underneath
questions.explanation: A protective aluminium-oxide layer forms quickly and stops further reaction.

questions.q: Ornaments are made of gold and silver rather than iron mainly because gold and silver:
options: Are shiny and do not corrode easily
questions.explanation: Gold and silver stay lustrous and resist corrosion, so they suit jewellery.
